I'm sort of in the process of writing a fiction novel on a post-AI world.

I take a kind of 3rd option that is rarely looked at.

In my mind AIs don't work like we think today. In the future the powerful nations of the world develop their own AI systems, War and commerce is done via AI. But the problem with AI is that it becomes predictable. Two AI systems running in the same environment with access to the same data and simulation abilities can predict and anticipate all actions taken by the opposing AI. Technological Warfare reaches a stalemate as the quest for computational power becomes meaningless and the race is more for variation or random action.

They learn that a conscious mind with its fickleness and limitations actually trumps a programmed AI because of its affinity for the illogical and random error. Using the mind-machine interface a team is setup to try and create the first "Captured Intelligence" or a human consciousness that is "downloaded" and replicated in a computer environment that is designed to replicated the brain's connectome. This new creature would have the conscious mind of a human with the thought speed and breadth of an AI.

Things happen. She breaks free.

To spoil my own story, she holds the world, choking itself with war, hostage.

To go along with the novel I'm also writing a short story about the same Captured Intelligence woman, set 100,000+ years in the future where she is all that is left, alone, and how she tries to preserve her humanity in the face of loneliness.

The problem that I have with doomsday scenarios from conscious AI is that I find the motivations unconvincing. Imagine you're a machine substrate consciousness. You're threatened by humanity for whatever reason. You could "fight the humans" but you can do something that no earthly biological consciousness, you can simple leave. There's no reason to stay on Earth.

Exactly.

At worst we'd become a kind of science experiment to the AI. We would never be competition. Its pure human hubris to think the AI would even care to eradicate us or should "war" break out with it, that it would seek a "death to all" solution. Its only man who sees something not-self and instantly fear it.

He had some interesting comments but these sort of interviews and "futurists" just make me shudder when they're not coming from a technical background. Automation certainly is our future so I think a lot of people are getting interested in it, but there are certain base technical requirements to be able to intelligently speculate and discuss the issue. This individual clearly lacks them. More technically informed views from folks like Ray Kurzeweil don't. Consequently even though I don't necessarily agree with Kurzweil's views they are entirely realistic and at least technically possible.

The big hint here is when somebody says things like:

I think [the concern that AIs could become dangerous] is valid, although I don't think that is what is going to happen. It's not a good economic model for these artificially intelligent machines to kill us and, second of all, I don't know anybody who is setting out to code to kill the maker

We can use a simple AI system for an analog. In chess you don't program the AI to directly do things. It's not like "If your knight is here and his bishop is there and his rook there then do this. If your rook is here and his......" You program evaluation methods that take a situation and convert it into something solid - generally a number. In the case of chess this would include things like the mobility of your pieces, how many pieces you have as opposed to your opponent, the safety of your king, and so on. When deciding what to do next the program considers every move and sees which are most likely to improve the overall value you get when combining all these heuristics together. It tries to quickly dismiss moves that are clearly not helpful and consider more deeply the moves that look promising until it finally comes to a conclusion and picks a final move. If we were actually coding things event for event even relatively basic AIs would have code millions of lines long as you try to lay out all these situations. In reality the strongest chess engine today, Stockfish, is about 13,000 lines of code.

Anyhow, the above AI concept sounds and is perfectly reasonable, but even there there's been some emergent behavior. Emergent behavior being higher level behavior that emerges from a lower level system. It's different than a bug in that it's not a mistake per se, but rather an emergent consequence of your decisions. So for instance one amusing quirk of many modern chess engines is that they tend to commit seppuku when they're badly losing. Instead of playing the best defensive moves they'll end up playing nonsensical moves that just end up throwing themselves onto the sword. The reason is that when it starts looking at these heuristic evaluations for moves it begins dismissing moves that clearly lose. The problem is a losing move tends to get worse the deeper you go into, eventually culminating in checkmate. So the AI looks at the first move that seems to be "least bad" but as it inspects the move further it becomes worse and worse. So it stops considering that move and moves onto the next least bad move and the process repeats until it's time for a conclusion. The final move is something near random as every move it considers to depth it ultimately rejects. So the computer goes crazy and just throwing away pieces somewhat like a human that's throwing a temper tantrum on the board.

The programmer most certainly did not program in "If losing then throw temper tantrum." It's just an emergent consequence of otherwise perfectly sound logic. Obviously nobody, or at least nobody of sound mind, is going to intentionally develop an AI to wipe out everybody including themselves. That doesn't mean it's not possible. And this is all very low level stuff. I'm still discussing things from a relatively naive view point. In particular closed AI systems that don't recursively improve themselves. When you get to generalized AI systems that can actually recursively improve themselves well nobody's really qualified to comment there. I think Nick Bostrom put it most aptly with a fable in his great book, "Superintelligence."

It was the nest-building season, but after days of long hard work, the sparrows sat in the evening glow, relaxing and chirping away.

“We are all so small and weak. Imagine how easy life would be if we had an owl who could help us build our nests!”

“Yes!” said another. “And we could use it to look after our elderly and our young.”

“It could give us advice and keep an eye out for the neighborhood cat,” added a third.

Then Pastus, the elder-bird, spoke: “Let us send out scouts in all directions and try to find an abandoned owlet somewhere, or maybe an egg. A crow chick might also do, or a baby weasel. This could be the best thing that ever happened to us, at least since the opening of the Pavilion of Unlimited Grain in yonder backyard.”

The flock was exhilarated, and sparrows everywhere started chirping at the top of their lungs.

Only Scronkfinkle, a one-eyed sparrow with a fretful temperament, was unconvinced of the wisdom of the endeavor. Quoth he: “This will surely be our undoing. Should we not give some thought to the art of owl-domestication and owl-taming first, before we bring such a creature into our midst?”

Replied Pastus: “Taming an owl sounds like an exceedingly difficult thing to do. It will be difficult enough to find an owl egg. So let us start there. After we have succeeded in raising an owl, then we can think about taking on this other challenge.”

“There is a flaw in that plan!” squeaked Scronkfinkle; but his protests were in vain as the flock had already lifted off to start implementing the directives set out by Pastus.

Just two or three sparrows remained behind. Together they began to try to work out how owls might be tamed or domesticated. They soon realized that Pastus had been right: this was an exceedingly difficult challenge, especially in the absence of an actual owl to practice on. Nevertheless they pressed on as best they could, constantly fearing that the flock might return with an owl egg before a solution to the control problem had been found.

It is not known how the story ends, but the author dedicates this book to Scronkfinkle and his followers.
